slides.title: Dispatch Copilot: launch it in a Pro tier in Q4 2027, after the mobile app, rather than as a $149 add-on in Q2

paragraphs.text: Brightwork  |  Executive team, January 2027 planning
Dispatch Copilot: launch it in a Pro tier in Q4 2027, after the mobile app, rather than as a $149 add-on in Q2
Recommendation on launch timing, packaging and price for CEO Maya Okafor and the executive team
Prepared November 2026 using only the internal briefing pack. All company, competitor and market figures are synthetic benchmark data. Figures are annual and in US$ unless stated.

slides.title: Executive summary: launch Copilot in Q4 2027 inside a new Pro tier at +$12 per seat, and keep the mobile rewrite on schedule

paragraphs.text: Executive summary: launch Copilot in Q4 2027 inside a new Pro tier at +$12 per seat, and keep the mobile rewrite on schedule

Answer: Yes, launch Dispatch Copilot, but in Q4 2027 rather than Q2, and inside a new Pro plan at $91 per seat ($12 above Core) with a pooled usage allowance. Plan on $1.2–2.9M of new ARR, not $8M. Copilot and the mobile fix are both needed to lift NRR to 105%.
Copilot is worth launching, but the prize is $1.2–2.9M of new ARR, not $8M
Only 14% of beta volunteers paid $149 when asked (17 of 120). The 46% survey figure comes from the 6% of admins who replied, and they run larger accounts
AI can explain at most the 7-point fall in win rate against Routewise: ~110 deals and $0.6M of new ARR a year, not a third of all losses
Package it in Pro at +$12 per seat with 600 requests per seat, not as a $149 add-on
Pro brings in as much ARR ($2.9M at the 33% uptake of the 2023 tier, vs $2.5M for the add-on). Its cost grows with seats, and it matches Routewise's 'AI included in Pro'
With the allowance, company gross margin stays at 75.9% or more in the worst usage case. Bundling Copilot free into Core would cut it to 71.9%
Launch in Q4 2027: fixing the mobile app comes first
Mobile reliability causes 27% of churn and AI features 6%. Two quarters of mobile delay put $0.5M–$1.1M of ARR at risk. Two quarters of Copilot delay put at most $0.6M at risk
Reaching 105% NRR takes both: the mobile fix adds about +1.9 pts and Copilot Pro adds +2.1 to +5.0 pts
Decisions for January: approve the sequence and the Pro design; run a paid early-access test in H1 2027; bring the launch forward to Q2 only if one of the triggers on slide 16 fires.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (Nov 2026); team analysis. Calculations on the slides that follow and in the appendix.

slides.title: We tested the CPO's plan against five conditions. Demand and timing failed, so the answer changed

paragraphs.text: We tested the CPO's plan against five conditions. Demand and timing failed, so the answer changed
Starting hypothesis (CPO): launch in Q2 2027 as a paid add-on at $149 per account per month, worth about $8M of ARR in year 1.

data: What would have to be true
Demand: about 46% of accounts will pay $149 a month
Paywall test: 17 of 120 beta volunteers (14%) bought. The survey had a 6% response rate, and respondents average 9.4 seats against 6.2 for the base
The add-on is worth $2.5M of ARR at most, not $8.1M
Economics: the price covers inference and company GM stays ≥75%
The add-on's own margin is 34% and company GM 76.2%. The top 10% of accounts cost $131 a month to serve against a $149 price
Price per seat and cap usage
Competition: AI is why we lose to Routewise
Win rate fell 7 points while Routewise was offering 20% off. 31% of loss notes 'mention' AI. AI is the main reason for only 6% of churn
At most $0.6M of new ARR a year is at stake
Opportunity cost: a two-quarter mobile delay costs less than a two-quarter Copilot delay
Mobile drives 27% of churn. A two-quarter delay puts $0.5M–$1.1M of ARR at risk, against ≤$0.6M for Copilot
Protect mobile and launch Copilot in Q4 2027
Proven value: beta gains will hold across the customer base
Beta: +11% jobs per dispatcher-hour vs +2% for matched accounts, and 97% vs 93% renewal. But the accounts volunteered and are larger (8.1 seats)
Leave retention upside out of the case and test it

paragraphs.text: Revised answer: launch in Q4 2027, after the mobile rewrite, inside a per-seat Pro tier with a usage allowance. Size the case at $1.2–2.9M, not $8M.
Source: Briefing pack §4–§8, §10; team analysis.

slides.title: Survey intent overstates demand: what customers actually paid points to at most $2.5M of add-on ARR, not $8M

paragraphs.text: 1  Is it worth launching?
2  Packaging and price
3  Timing
4  Risks and next steps
Survey intent overstates demand: what customers actually paid points to at most $2.5M of add-on ARR, not $8M
Year-1 add-on ARR at $149 a month, by adoption source ($M)
Why the 46% does not translate into revenue
Few people answered, and they were not typical. Only 610 of 9,800 admins (6%) replied. They average 9.4 seats against 6.2 for the base, so the sample leans to large, engaged accounts
Saying 'likely' is not buying. When the 120 beta accounts were actually asked to pay $149, 17 did (14%), less than a third of the survey's 46%
14% is a ceiling, not a base case. Beta accounts volunteered and are larger (8.1 seats) and more active than the base, so the base will convert at a lower rate
Buyers are heavy users. Those who paid averaged 6,800 requests a month, almost twice the beta mean of 3,600. That raises the cost of serving them (slide 8)
So what: plan on $1.2–2.5M from a $149 add-on and test conversion on a random sample of accounts that did not volunteer
How the numbers are built
Survey: 9,800 × 46% = 4,508 accounts × $1,788 a year = $8.1M
Paywall: 9,800 × 14% = 1,372 accounts × $1,788 a year = $2.5M
Non-volunteer case: 9,800 × 7% = 686 accounts × $1,788 a year = $1.2M
Source: Briefing pack §4, §6, §10 (survey method note), §5. ARR = accounts × $149 × 12. The 7% case is our illustrative haircut for the fact that beta accounts volunteered.

slides.title: Against Routewise, Copilot can win back at most ~110 deals a year (about $0.6M of ARR), not a third of our losses

paragraphs.text: 1  Is it worth launching?
2  Packaging and price
3  Timing
4  Risks and next steps
Against Routewise, Copilot can win back at most ~110 deals a year (about $0.6M of ARR), not a third of our losses
Brightwork win rate in deals where Routewise competes (%)
Why the competitive upside is real but limited
The VP Sales claim fails a basic check. Winning back a third of our losses would lift the win rate to 58%, 14 points higher than before Routewise had any AI
Mentioning AI is not the same as losing on AI. 31% of Q3 loss notes mention AI, but a note can mention it without AI deciding the deal
Price is a competing explanation. Routewise offered 20% off the first year in the same quarter it launched AI, and price already causes 22% of our churn
So $0.6M a year is the most Copilot can be worth here, and it counts as new-customer growth, not NRR
A test is available by January. Q4 2026 win rates come after the promo ended. If they stay at or below 37%, AI is the likely cause, and that would make launching sooner more urgent
How the numbers are built
2,600 opportunities × 60% = 1,560 Routewise deals a year
7-pt drop × 1,560 = 109 deals × $5,878 = $0.64M of new ARR a year
VP claim: 1/3 × 983 losses = 328 deals → 58% win rate
Source: Briefing pack §7, §10 (VP Sales memo), §11. New account = 6.2 seats × $79 × 12 = $5,878 ARR. Pre-AI win rate assumed to be the Q1–Q2 2026 rate.

slides.title: A flat $149 price attracts heavy users: serving the top 10% of accounts would use up 88% of the price in inference alone

A flat $149 price attracts heavy users: serving the top 10% of accounts would use up 88% of the price in inference alone
Inference cost per account per month vs the $149 add-on price ($)
Why per-seat pricing is the better structure
A flat price selects for heavy use. The accounts that paid used almost twice the beta mean, because they get the most from a fixed fee
Pricing per seat follows usage. Usage grows with dispatcher seats: $4.00 of inference per seat against a $12 price leaves 67% before platform cost
Smaller accounts pay less. A typical 6.2-seat account pays $74 a month for Pro instead of $149. That matters when price causes 22% of churn
So what: charge per seat and set an allowance, so that one heavy account cannot turn the feature unprofitable
Margin left after inference at $149
Break-even: $149 ÷ $0.009 = 16,556 requests a month. Any account above that loses money
Source: Briefing pack §5 Table 2, §6. Inference cost = requests per month × $0.009. Per-seat figure = 3,600 requests ÷ 8.1 beta seats = 444 requests per seat.

Company gross margin above (+) or below (−) the 75% floor, percentage points
Why the allowance matters
Without an allowance, Pro could breach the floor. If upgraders behave like the paywall buyers, company GM falls to 74.1%
600 requests per seat caps the downside. That is $5.40 of inference against $12, so company GM stays at 75.9% or more whatever the usage mix
Typical users never hit it. The beta average is 444 requests per seat, and the median account used about 235 per seat
Margin improves after 2027. Our $0.009 rate is fixed through December 2027, and the provider's list prices fell 35% last year. Re-price at renewal

slides.title: A two-quarter delay to the mobile rewrite puts up to twice as much ARR at risk as a two-quarter delay to Copilot

paragraphs.text: 1  Is it worth launching?
2  Packaging and price
3  Timing
4  Risks and next steps
A two-quarter delay to the mobile rewrite puts up to twice as much ARR at risk as a two-quarter delay to Copilot
ARR permanently lost during a two-quarter delay ($M)
Why mobile goes first
Losses to churn are permanent. An account that leaves while we wait for the mobile app does not come back when it ships
Copilot revenue is mostly postponed, not lost. Accounts that would take Pro in Q2 can take it in Q4. Six months of deferral costs $0.1M–$0.7M of gross profit
The threshold is not demanding. The rewrite only has to fix 26–52% of the churn caused by the app's reliability
The engineering cost is the same in either order. $1.47M. Only the sequence changes
So what: do the mobile rewrite first, unless the January data shows AI is costing us deals (slide 16)

categories: Delay mobile: rewrite fixes all mobile churn
Delay Copilot: full credit for win rate + AI churn

paragraphs.text: How the numbers are built
Copilot: ($0.64M win-rate gap + $0.48M AI churn) × 0.5 yr = $0.56M; half credit = $0.28M
Break-even: mobile-first wins if the rewrite fixes more than 52% (full credit) or 26% (half credit) of mobile churn

Source: Briefing pack §3, §7, §8, §9; team analysis. Six months = 0.5 × annual figure. 'Half credit' assumes the Routewise promo explains half of the win-rate drop and Copilot prevents half of AI churn. Engineering cost: 14 × $210k × 0.5 yr = $1.47M in either order.
